title: Agribusiness and Farm Management Basics
summary: Learn the agricultural value chain, soil and inputs, farm records and gross margins, post-harvest storage, marketing and finance, and climate-smart farming, with worked farm calculations.
audience: Farmers, agricultural students, extension workers and agri-entrepreneurs

lessons.title: Agriculture as a business: the value chain

body.p: Agribusiness means running farming and the activities around it as a business: supplying inputs, producing crops and livestock, processing, transporting, storing and selling food and fibre. Agriculture employs a large share of workers across Africa, and most food is still grown on small farms, so better farm business skills raise incomes and food security at the same time.

list: Inputs: seed, fertiliser, feed, tools, finance and advice.
Production: growing crops or raising animals on the farm.
Aggregation and storage: collecting produce from many farmers and keeping it safe.
Processing: milling maize, making cheese, drying mangoes, packing vegetables.
Distribution and retail: transport, markets, supermarkets and export.
Consumers: whose preferences and prices drive the whole chain.

body.p: Value is added at each step. A farmer who sells raw cassava earns far less per kilogram than one who sells dried, packaged gari. Finding where you can add value, cut losses or reach better buyers is the core skill of agribusiness.

body.tip: Start by mapping your own chain: who supplies you, who buys from you, and where the biggest price jumps happen.

body.p: Healthy soil is the farm's main asset. Crops need nitrogen (N) for leaves, phosphorus (P) for roots and early growth and potassium (K) for strength and quality, plus water, organic matter and a suitable pH. A soil test tells you what is missing so you do not waste money on fertiliser you do not need.

Fertiliser grades show the percentage of N, P and K (often written as N-P₂O₅-K₂O). A 50 kg bag of 20-10-10 contains 50 x 0.20 = 10 kg of nitrogen and 5 kg each of the phosphate and potash nutrients. If a maize crop needs 60 kg of nitrogen per hectare, that is 60 / 10 = 6 bags per hectare, ideally split between planting and top-dressing.

list: Choose certified seed of varieties suited to your rainfall and market.
Plant at the recommended spacing and time; late planting often cuts yield sharply.
Rotate crops (for example maize after beans) to restore nitrogen and break pest cycles.
Use integrated pest management: scouting, resistant varieties and pesticides only when needed, used exactly as the label says.

body.tip: Keep manure and crop residues on the field where you can. Organic matter holds water and nutrients and improves the return on fertiliser.

lessons.title: Farm records, costs and gross margin

body.p: Without records, a farmer cannot know which crop or field makes money. Record every input bought, every hour of hired labour, yields per field and every sale. Simple notebooks or free phone apps are enough to start.

Gross margin = revenue - variable costs. Variable costs change with the size of the enterprise: seed, fertiliser, chemicals, hired labour, fuel and transport. Example: 2 hectares of maize yield 4 tonnes per hectare, sold at R3500 a tonne, so revenue = 2 x 4 x 3500 = R28 000. Variable costs are R9000 per hectare, R18 000 in total. Gross margin = R10 000, or R5000 per hectare.

The break-even yield covers variable costs exactly: 18 000 / 3500 is about 5.14 tonnes in total, or about 2.57 tonnes per hectare. In a drought year with a yield below that, the crop loses money. Fixed costs (land rent, equipment, insurance) must also be covered from the gross margins of all enterprises together.

list: Compare enterprises by gross margin per hectare or per unit of scarce resource (such as water or labour).
Raising yield from 2.5 to 4 tonnes per hectare is a 60% increase, often worth more than a small price rise.
Review records after each season and plan the next one from them.

body.tip: Count family labour and your own time too, even if you do not pay it in cash; otherwise a crop can look more profitable than it is.

body.p: Large shares of harvests are lost after they leave the field: grain to insects, moulds and rodents, fruit and vegetables to bruising and heat. If a cooperative loses 20% of 100 tonnes of grain worth R3000 a tonne, it throws away 100 x 0.2 x 3000 = R60 000.

list: Harvest at the right maturity and handle produce gently.
Dry grain to a safe moisture content before storage; damp grain grows mould, which can produce dangerous aflatoxins.
Store in clean, raised, ventilated stores or airtight hermetic bags that starve insects of oxygen.
Cool fresh produce quickly; shade and evaporative coolers help where cold rooms are unavailable.

body.p: Prices are often lowest at harvest. Suppose 10 tonnes sell for R3000 a tonne at harvest (R30 000). Stored for four months, 2% is lost and storage costs R150 a tonne, but the price rises to R3900. Income = 9.8 x 3900 - 10 x 150 = R36 720, R6720 more than selling at harvest. The gain depends on prices really rising and losses staying low, so weigh the risk.

body.tip: Warehouse receipt systems let farmers store grain in certified warehouses and borrow against it, without selling at the harvest low.

body.p: Selling well is as important as growing well. Know your buyers' standards (size, grade, moisture, packaging), compare prices across markets and seasons, and build relationships with reliable buyers.

list: Cooperatives and farmer groups bulk produce, share transport and bargain for better prices and input discounts.
Contract farming: a buyer agrees in advance to buy at a set price or formula, sometimes supplying inputs; read the terms on quality and payment carefully.
Processing and branding add value and extend shelf life.
Digital platforms and mobile money connect farmers to buyers and speed up payment.

body.p: Loans can pay for inputs that raise yields, but borrowing must be planned against expected cash flow. A loan of R20 000 at 18% simple annual interest for 6 months costs 20 000 x 0.18 x 0.5 = R1800, so R21 800 must be repaid after harvest. Crop or livestock insurance, including index insurance based on rainfall, protects against disasters.

body.tip: Prepare a simple budget and cash-flow plan before approaching a lender; it shows you understand when money comes in and goes out.

body.p: Changing rainfall, droughts, floods and heat waves already affect farms. Climate-smart agriculture aims to raise productivity, help farms adapt, and cut emissions where possible.

list: Conservation agriculture: minimal tillage, permanent soil cover and crop rotation to save soil and moisture.
Drought-tolerant and early-maturing varieties.
Water harvesting: tied ridges, planting pits and small dams.
Agroforestry: trees that give shade, fodder, fruit and nitrogen.
Diversifying crops and livestock so one failure does not ruin the household.

body.p: Irrigation methods differ in how much pumped water reaches the roots. If a crop needs 2500 m³ of water at the roots, drip irrigation at about 90% efficiency needs about 2500 / 0.9 = 2778 m³, while flood irrigation at 50% needs 5000 m³. Drip costs more to install but saves water, pumping energy and often raises yields.
Sustainable practices also protect markets: many buyers and export markets now ask how food was produced, and good records of practices can open premium markets.

body.tip: Use weather forecasts and advisory services by SMS or radio to time planting, spraying and harvesting.

quiz.q: What is an agricultural value chain?
options: All the steps from inputs to the consumer

quiz.q: A 50 kg bag of 20-10-10 fertiliser contains how much nitrogen?
A crop needs 60 kg N per hectare. How many 50 kg bags of 20-10-10 per hectare?

options: It removes the need for any inputs
Beans add nitrogen and rotation breaks pest cycles

quiz.q: 2 ha of maize yield 4 t/ha sold at R3500/t. What is the revenue?
With variable costs of R18 000, what is the gross margin?
What is the break-even yield per hectare at R3500/t with R9000/ha variable costs?
A cooperative loses 20% of 100 t of grain worth R3000/t. What is the loss?
Why must grain be dried before storage?
options: Damp grain grows moulds that can produce aflatoxins

quiz.q: Storing 10 t (2% loss, R150/t cost) and selling at R3900 instead of R3000 earns how much more?
What is a main benefit of joining a cooperative?
options: Bulking produce to bargain for better prices

quiz.q: A R20 000 loan at 18% simple annual interest for 6 months costs how much interest?
A crop needs 2500 m³ at the roots. How much water must drip irrigation (90% efficient) supply?

options: Conservation agriculture with soil cover and rotation
Planting one crop only every year
